source.title_on_document: Is ChatGPT detrimental to innovation? A field experiment among university students

supplement.where: Supporting documents containing the experimental script and consent screenshot (PDF p. 9, Methods, lines 196-198); S1 experimental script (PDF p. 11, lines 238-239); appendix II (PDF p. 14, Results, lines 300-301). No direct supplement URL is supplied in the saved PDF.
supplement.holds: The experimental script and consent material, and additional innovation tests described as statistically insignificant. Appendix II is absent, so its outcome definitions, statistics and any additional standard errors cannot be confirmed. Main-text Figure 1 through Figure 6 and Table 1 through Table 4 are present as appended image pages; the innovation regression coefficients and parenthesized uncertainty are in Table 2, PDF p. 30.

paper_design_summary: Senior Egyptian undergraduates in two existing courses wrote three graded essays over one month with ChatGPT or without it; the authors call course enrollment the unit of randomization (PDF p. 8, Methods). One week after the assignments, the same sample completed a laboratory lemonade-stand game including advertising slogans, together with risk and effort tasks (PDF pp. 9-11, Methods). Creativity-related analyses assessed variation in each participant's sales strategies and human-rated slogan creativity (PDF pp. 12-14, Results).

studies.label: Course-level ChatGPT essay intervention followed by a laboratory innovation game

assignment.what_was_assigned: The authors report course-level randomization: enrollment in Social Network Analysis determined the ChatGPT essay arm and enrollment in Data Mining determined the control arm. The courses were existing groups; people were not individually randomized. The mechanism for randomly selecting which course received ChatGPT is not described. The field_rct classification follows the explicit randomization claim, with this limitation retained for audit.
assignment.quote: We used the enrollment in either of these two courses as our unit of randomization to assign participants to either the treatment or the control.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 8, Methods, lines 169-181; PDF p. 17, Discussion, lines 371-377.
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF p. 7, Methods, lines 154-155, explicitly calls the experiment pre-registered; also PDF p. 16, Discussion, lines 360-363. No registration identifier, link or registered outcome hierarchy is given.

arms.name: ChatGPT essays (Social Network Analysis course)
arms.description: Students enrolled in Social Network Analysis were asked to write the essay assignments using ChatGPT (PDF p. 8, Methods, lines 176-181); researchers created accounts for them (PDF p. 9, lines 182-189). Table 1 reports 50 people in this arm before the additional outlier exclusions (PDF p. 29); its final analyzed arm count is not reported.

arms.name: No-ChatGPT essays (Data Mining course)
arms.description: Students enrolled in Data Mining completed the essay assignments with ChatGPT neither mentioned nor allowed (PDF p. 8, Methods, lines 176-181). Table 1 reports 43 people in this arm before the additional outlier exclusions (PDF p. 29); its final analyzed arm count is not reported.

participants.exclusions: The paper reports 94 initially recruited, not a count specifically at random assignment. One subject was discarded for missing information during payouts (PDF p. 11, Results, lines 242-244). Table 1 contains 93 people: control 43 and ChatGPT 50 (PDF p. 29, Observations row). Two further anomalous observations were removed using the 1.5xIQR rule (PDF p. 12, lines 254-256); Tables 2 and 3 report 91 observations (PDF pp. 30-31). The excluded subjects' arms and final analyzed counts by arm are not stated. The main outcome-analysis total is recorded as 91; the pre-outlier demographic counts are not used as final arm counts.
participants.who: Senior undergraduates at an Egyptian public university, with a social-sciences major and social science computing minor, enrolled in Social Network Analysis or Data Mining (PDF pp. 7-8, Methods, lines 154-155 and 169-171).
participants.quote: A total of 94 subjects were initially recruited for the experiment. However, one subject was discarded due to missing information during payouts.
participants.locator: PDF pp. 7-8, Methods; PDF p. 11, Results, lines 242-244; PDF p. 12, lines 254-256; PDF p. 29, Table 1; PDF p. 30, Table 2, Observations row.

ai_tool.how_used: The treatment students were asked to use ChatGPT to write their graded essay assignments. Researchers created accounts using foreign cell phone numbers because local access was unavailable during the intervention. Specific prompts, model, usage logs and interaction constraints are not reported (PDF pp. 8-9, Methods, lines 176-189). The laboratory outcomes followed this essay-use period rather than being scored from the AI-assisted essays.

task.description: The treatment phase involved graded course essays. The outcome task was a hypothetical lemonade-stand business strategy game: choose stand location, lemonade color, sugar content, lemon concentration and price, and write an advertising message or slogan of at most 20 words. Participants could retain or change strategies after receiving profit feedback. The slogan component is creative writing; the strategy component tests exploratory business problem solving. The slogans did not affect payoffs (PDF p. 10, Methods, lines 204-223).
task.duration: Three graded essays over one month during term time in April 2023 (PDF p. 8, lines 176-181); laboratory follow-up one week after submission (PDF p. 9, lines 190-191); seven game rounds (PDF p. 10, lines 204-206). Session duration in minutes is not stated.

outcomes.name: Creativity of lemonade-stand advertising messages
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Four external annotators, unaware of the research question and experimental design, rated advertising messages produced during the laboratory game. Methods gives a creativity scale from 0 to 10 (PDF p. 10, lines 218-223), whereas Results gives an innovation scale from 1 to 10 (PDF p. 14, lines 295-298). Results reports 265 unique messages because participants sometimes retained a message between rounds. These are outputs, not participants. The message is the stated scoring unit; aggregation across raters and messages, and the exact observational unit and sample size of the Mann-Whitney test, are not specified. Figure 3 supplies graphical arm levels and error bars without numerical labels or a definition of the bars. No primary-outcome hierarchy is stated.
outcomes.delay: One week after all essay assignments were submitted (PDF p. 9, Methods, lines 190-191). The later laboratory task is described separately from the ChatGPT essay intervention; an explicit laboratory access prohibition is not reproduced in this PDF.

contrasts.reported: Mann Whitney U test, p-value > 0.05. The paper reports 265 unique messages rated by four coders. Figure 3 displays arm-level creativity scores and error bars but no printed numerical arm means, SDs, or intervals; no graph values have been estimated.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 14, Results, lines 295-302; PDF p. 25, Figure 3; rating procedure: PDF p. 10, Methods, lines 218-223.

outcomes.name: Aggregate exploration of lemonade-stand sales strategies
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Computed within-person variation in chosen strategies across the game. The paper describes the aggregate as the average, subject-specific standard deviation of sugar content, lemon concentration and price (PDF p. 13, lines 272-276); the game has seven rounds (PDF p. 10, lines 204-213). Coded as flexibility because it measures variation within one participant, not similarity across different people. The automated_score code denotes the computed dispersion score, not an AI judge. Table 2 reports an unadjusted model and a model controlling for female, age, urban residence and financial status; these are variants of this same outcome. Its note says results are clustered by Subject ID, although assignment was by course. Figure 2 has graphical levels and error bars with no numerical labels or definition of the bars. The text describes the effect as approximately 0.6 to 0.72 standard deviation points, but does not document standardization by a between-participant outcome SD; these coefficients are not treated as confirmed standardized effect sizes.
outcomes.delay: One week after all essay assignments were submitted (PDF p. 9, Methods, lines 190-191). The later laboratory task is described separately from the ChatGPT essay intervention; an explicit laboratory access prohibition is not reproduced in this PDF.

contrasts.reported: Table 2, ChatGPT row: model (1) -0.719** (0.326); model (2) -0.604* (0.328). Observations: 91 in each model. Parenthesized values are transcribed as the reported regression uncertainty. Table note: Results are clustered by Subject ID, *** p<0.01, ** p<0.05, * p<0.1. Results text: Mann Whitney U test, p-value = 0.037; the prose describes a decrease of approximately 0.6 to 0.72 standard deviation points. Figure 2 shows lower aggregate exploration for ChatGPT, without printed numerical arm means or intervals.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 30, Table 2, ChatGPT row, Observations row and note; PDF p. 13, Results, lines 272-294; PDF p. 24, Figure 2.

outcomes.name: Exploration of lemon concentration
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Subject-specific standard deviation of the lemon-concentration choices across the laboratory game, reported separately as a component outcome in Figure 1. The choice scale is 0 to 10 (PDF p. 10, Methods, lines 204-213); the innovation-score definition and separate parameter tests are in PDF p. 12, Results, lines 258-269. This is within-person variation, not diversity across people. Figure 1 supplies arm-level point estimates and error bars, but numerical arm values and the definition of the bars are not stated.
outcomes.delay: One week after all essay assignments were submitted (PDF p. 9, Methods, lines 190-191). The later laboratory task is described separately from the ChatGPT essay intervention; an explicit laboratory access prohibition is not reproduced in this PDF.

contrasts.reported: Mann Whitney p-value=0.036. Figure 1, lemon concentration panel, shows a lower subject-specific SD for ChatGPT than for control. Numerical arm means, SDs and intervals are not printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 12, Results, lines 258-269; PDF p. 23, Figure 1, lemon concentration panel.

company_involvement.description: No company authorship, funding or other company involvement is reported. Author affiliations and acknowledgments name academic/public institutions; use of ChatGPT alone is not coded as company involvement.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1, author affiliations; PDF p. 18, Acknowledgments.

eligibility.reason: Eligible on the authors' explicit report of course-level randomization to ChatGPT versus no ChatGPT (PDF p. 8, Methods, lines 169-181), 91 people in the main outcome analyses (PDF p. 30, Table 2), and creativity scored by external annotators on participants' own advertising messages (PDF p. 10, Methods, lines 218-223; PDF p. 14, Results). The later laboratory outputs answer after_ai. This is a reported cluster-randomized field intervention with laboratory follow-up, not individual randomization or an AI-versus-human output comparison. The course-allocation mechanism remains undocumented, and subject-level clustering of Table 2 uncertainty does not reflect the course-level assignment (PDF p. 30, table note); core inclusion here does not establish suitability of that precision for pooling.

one_line_finding: One week after the essay intervention, prior ChatGPT users showed less variation in sales strategies (ChatGPT coefficient -0.719, parenthesized uncertainty 0.326, N = 91; PDF p. 30, Table 2, model 1), while slogan creativity showed no clear difference (Mann Whitney U p-value > 0.05; PDF p. 14, Results; PDF p. 25, Figure 3).
open_questions: Confirm the course-allocation procedure: the authors call course enrollment the unit of randomization but do not describe a random draw assigning the two existing courses to arms (PDF p. 8, Methods; PDF p. 17, Discussion). The field_rct/yes coding follows that claim; if course assignment was purposive, quasi_people and observational context would apply.

Obtain the cited S1/supporting documents and Appendix II to identify additional innovation outcomes, their statistics, the experimental instructions, and any preregistration details. They are absent from this PDF (references at PDF pp. 9, 11 and 14).

Confirm laboratory AI-access restrictions and whether students could continue using their supplied accounts during the interval. after_ai/no availability is coded from the described sequence of the prior essay intervention and later laboratory tests, and the stated interest in domains where ChatGPT is not used; an explicit laboratory prohibition is not printed (PDF pp. 5 and 8-10).

Obtain the post-exclusion analyzed counts by arm and outcome. Table 1 has 93 demographic observations, whereas the main regressions have 91 after the additional outlier removals (PDF pp. 11-12, 29-31).

Resolve whether aggregate exploration is an average or another aggregation of the parameter-specific SDs, and whether any between-participant standardization was performed; the raw scale must be established before treating the prose description of 0.6 to 0.72 standard deviation points as a standardized effect (PDF pp. 13, 23-24 and 30). Course-level rather than subject-level uncertainty also needs review.

Resolve the advertising-message rating scale (0 to 10 in Methods versus 1 to 10 in Results), the aggregation over raters/messages/participants, the actual test sample, and the definitions of figure error bars (PDF pp. 10, 14 and 25).

The local filename/candidate record identifies a later journal version, but the saved PDF is the April 5, 2024 preprint. Differences in the journal version have not been verified; all screening numbers here are from the saved PDF.
notes: Screened 2026-10-09. Read the complete markdown conversion, including its ending material, and checked the PDF tables/figures directly. All locators refer to physical PDF pages: main text and references occupy pp. 1-22; Figures 1-6 are on pp. 23-28; Tables 1-4 are on pp. 29-32. The appended figures/tables are raster images with no usable table text, so they were inspected as images rendered in memory. Outcome inventory: Figure 1 reports lemon, sugar and price exploration; Figure 2 and Table 2 report aggregate exploration; Figure 3 reports message creativity; Figure 4 and Table 3 report risk-loving behavior; Figure 6 and Table 4 report effort through voluntary strategy-sheet completion. Figure 5 is the blank effort sheet, not another outcome, and Table 1 gives demographics. Risk and effort are not creativity/diversity scores on creative output and are therefore documented here but omitted from the coded outcomes. The three parameter-specific tests are retained as separately reported component outcomes; adjusted and unadjusted regression variants are combined under the aggregate outcome. Appendix II is said to contain other nonsignificant innovation tests, but their names and statistics cannot be recovered from this PDF. No across-people diversity measure or scored creativity result for the intervention essays is reported. This is one sample and one intervention with later follow-up, not separate field and laboratory studies. No reuse of another paper's participants is stated; the cited earlier lemonade-stand experiment supplies the game design (PDF p. 10), not an identified shared sample. Preregistration is claimed but no primary-outcome hierarchy is available. No effect size, numerical graph value or missing participant count was calculated.
